e.t: This Greek LXX noun means “exultation” or “joyfulness”—a strong, outward expression of gladness. It describes joyful celebration rather than merely quiet satisfaction, and it can name the gladness a person experiences or expresses. The word occurs 18 times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in 18 verses, appearing especially often in Psalms and once in Isaiah. Its normal sense remains focused on rejoicing and glad celebration; the surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis falls on the feeling itself or its outward expression.

This Greek LXX noun expresses the idea of being “untamed” or “unconquerable.” It describes something that has not been brought under control or defeated. The word therefore points to firmness or resistance rather than weakness or submission. It occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, all within Amos 7:7–8. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains something resistant to being mastered.

This word is the proper name “Azōtos; Azotos.” It identifies a named person, place, or other entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or relationship. Because it is a proper name, its meaning is primarily identification: it points readers to Azotos wherever it appears in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek scriptural books. It occurs 26 times in this LXX corpus, showing repeated reference to the same named entity across several books. The surrounding verse is needed to explain what is happening at each occurrence.

This verb means “hemorrhage,” describing the act or condition of bleeding. It functions as an action word rather than a title for a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Leviticus 15:33. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the occurrence of hemorrhaging or abnormal bleeding.

This noun means “anything used for anointing; unguent”—a substance applied in anointing. It refers to an oil, ointment, or similar preparation used for that purpose, rather than to the act of anointing itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Exodus 30:31 and Isaiah 61:3. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This verb means “raise,” describing the action of lifting something or someone upward. It presents raising as an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the LXX corpus, it occurs once, at Judges 16:3. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central meaning remains the act of raising or lifting. It is therefore a straightforward action word with a clear, limited occurrence in the Greek Old Testament.

This verb means “breathe again” or “take breath.” It describes the act of drawing breath, especially after a pause or difficulty. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 9:18, so its normal lexical sense is clear even though the supplied verse text is not available here. The word functions as an action rather than a person, object, or quality. Its precise force in Job 9:18 depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains renewed breathing or gaining breath.

This verb means “exchange”: it describes one thing being given in place of another, or people exchanging something with each other. It functions as an action word, focusing on the act of making that substitution or trade rather than on a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in Sirach and 3 Maccabees. The surrounding verse determines what is being exchanged.

This adjective describes something as “full of caves.” It refers to a place or feature marked by caves, emphasizing its cave-filled character rather than an action or person. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 2:5. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning is a clear description of a cave-filled location or object.

This verb means to hide something away, putting it out of sight or keeping it concealed. It can describe the act of withdrawing or concealing a person or thing rather than leaving it openly visible. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented by this LXX corpus, the word occurs 16 times, showing repeated use for concealment or removal from view. Its exact force in any verse depends on what is being hidden and the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX verb means to leave off or desist from something. It describes stopping an action rather than continuing it. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Daniel 5:26. As a verb, it expresses the act of ceasing, withdrawing, or refraining, while the surrounding sentence identifies what is being brought to an end. Its precise force in that verse depends on the wording and context of the passage.

This verb means “inactive,” describing a person or thing that is not working, acting, or carrying on its activity. It presents inactivity as the central idea rather than naming a particular object or event. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times, in Ezra, Ecclesiastes, Sirach, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on what the surrounding sentence says is inactive, but the basic meaning remains a lack of activity or action.

Aroukaios, also rendered Arukeos, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person or named individual in the Greek Old Testament translation. This name occurs once in the Septuagint, in Genesis 10:17. Because no verse text or surrounding context is provided here, its precise role in that passage cannot be described further; the lexical meaning is simply the personal name itself.

This Greek LXX verb means “resemble”: to be like someone or something in appearance or character. It describes likeness rather than identity, so the thing resembling another is presented as similar to it. The word occurs four times in the Greek text of the Epistle of Jeremiah, across three verses. Its exact force in any one passage depends on what is being compared, but its central idea remains becoming or being like another.

Baana, also rendered Vaana, is a personal name rather than a word describing an object, action, or quality. It identifies people in the Greek Old Testament and functions as a proper name wherever it appears. This name occurs 13 times in the LXX, across books including 2 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, and 1 Kings. Its precise reference depends on the person named in each passage.

Baiphalad, also rendered Vefalath, is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament translation. It refers to a named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. This LXX form appears once, in Joshua 15:27, so its meaning is primarily the identification of that name. No broader lexical sense is established by this single occurrence within the Greek Old Testament corpus.

This word is a proper name, referring to Begethon, also rendered Veyethon. It is not a general term describing an action, quality, or object, but a name used to identify a particular place or named entity. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 19:44. The available wording establishes the name, while the surrounding verse is needed to explain its specific role there.

This adverb means “for a while” or “little,” expressing a short duration or a small extent. It can describe something lasting only briefly, or something limited in amount or degree. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times, all in 2 Maccabees and 4 Maccabees. Its precise emphasis—brief time or limited measure—comes from the sentence where it appears.

This word is a proper name rendered as “Gad” or “Gath.” In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a named person, tribe, or place depending on the passage, rather than expressing an action or general quality. It occurs 79 times across 77 Old Testament verses, with many occurrences in Joshua and Numbers. The precise person or location it identifies must be determined from the surrounding passage.

Gothom is a personal name preserved in the Greek Septuagint. It is not presented here as a common word describing an action, quality, or object, but as the name of an individual. The name occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in Genesis 36, at Genesis 36:11 and Genesis 36:16. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific family relationship or role cannot be explained from the name alone.

This noun means “writing-tablet,” referring to a tablet used for writing or preserving written words. It names a physical writing surface rather than an action, person, or message itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times, all in 1 Maccabees. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a tablet associated with writing.

This word is a proper name, represented as “Dēlos” or “Thilos.” It does not describe a general quality, action, or object; it identifies a particular named entity in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings. The name occurs nine times in the LXX corpus, appearing in five Old Testament verses and four deuterocanonical verses. Its precise referent in any given passage must be determined from that passage’s surrounding text.

This verb means “dissipate” or “disperse”: it describes something being scattered or spread apart rather than remaining gathered. It appears eight times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is established across several scriptural settings. The surrounding passage determines what is being dispersed in any particular verse, but the word itself centers on separation, scattering, or breaking up of what was together.

This verb means to “dig through” something or to “undermine” it. It describes breaking into or through a barrier by digging, and it can also express the weakening or compromising of something. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times: once in Job and three times in Ezekiel. Its exact force in any particular sentence depends on what is being dug through or undermined, but the central idea remains penetrating or weakening a barrier.

This adjective means “two thousand,” expressing a quantity of 2,000 people, objects, or other counted things. It describes a number rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 40 times, appearing in both the Old Testament collection and the deuterocanonical books. Its exact wording in an English Bible may be divided between expressions such as a number and the thing being counted, but its underlying numerical meaning remains two thousand.

This adjective describes something burdensome—difficult to carry, bear, or endure. It presents a person, task, condition, or demand as placing a heavy load on someone rather than as easy or light. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Proverbs 34:3. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central idea remains a weight that is hard to bear.

Edeni, also rendered Etheni, is a proper name. It functions as a personal name rather than a general description, object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Numbers 26:40. Because the available text does not include the surrounding verse, the name’s specific role in that passage cannot be described further here. Its core meaning is therefore its identifying name: Edeni or Etheni.

This noun refers to vindication or vengeance—the setting right of a wrong through a decisive act of judgment. It can describe the answering of injustice, whether by defending what is right or by bringing deserved repayment against wrongdoing. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, it occurs 85 times, so it has a broad role in passages about justice and judgment. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX verb means “disturb”: to unsettle, trouble, or disrupt someone or something. It describes an action that disturbs a person’s peace or causes disorder, rather than simply referring to a quiet or inactive state. The word appears five times in the Greek Old Testament and related Wisdom writings, including two occurrences in Psalms and three in Wisdom. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being disturbed and the surrounding passage.

This adjective describes someone or something as “virtuous”—marked by moral excellence or worthy character. It functions as a describing word rather than naming a person, object, or action. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 11:5. The word’s basic sense is clear from its definition, while the surrounding verse would determine precisely what person or thing is being described there.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “defer” or “humiliate.” It can describe showing someone respect or yielding to that person, and it can also describe putting someone to shame or lowering them. The surrounding sentence determines which sense is intended. It occurs 40 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical books represented in this corpus, so it is used for more than one kind of human response or treatment.

This LXX noun means “concealment,” referring to the act or condition of hiding something from view. It names concealment rather than describing a person or action by itself. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament represented by this LXX corpus, in Exodus, 2 Samuel, and Job. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word means “success”: achieving a desired result or experiencing a favorable outcome. It is a noun, so it names the result or condition of succeeding rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs once, in Wisdom 13:19. The surrounding verse is needed to determine what kind of success is meant there; the word itself gives the general idea of a favorable result.

This noun refers to a saddleback or a coffer, a chest or container. Its meaning is associated with a physical object rather than an action or personal quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all in 1 Samuel. The wording is rendered “coffer” in two of its occurrences, while the lexical sense also includes “saddleback.” The precise reference may depend on the surrounding passage, but the word’s ordinary sense points to a tangible object used or carried in the narrative.

This Greek LXX noun means “favor”: goodwill, approval, or a positive disposition shown toward someone. It describes the favorable regard a person may receive or extend, rather than an action by itself. The word appears 17 times in the Greek LXX corpus, including passages in Esther and the Maccabean books. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and situation.

This adjective means “thankful”: it describes a person or attitude marked by gratitude. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Proverbs 11:16. The word presents thankfulness as a quality rather than an action or object. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains clear: someone or something characterized by gratitude. It is not a general term for every kind of approval or praise.

Zaphōim is a proper name, given in the Greek Old Testament as “Zaphōim; Zafim.” Unlike a common noun, it does not describe a general quality, action, or object; it identifies a particular named entity. This word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Genesis 36:43. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the specific identity or role associated with the name must be determined from that passage’s context.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Ēnan” or “Inan.” It identifies a person named in the Greek Old Testament text. The name appears once, in Nehemiah 10:27, and its role there is simply as a personal designation. No broader ordinary meaning, action, or quality is supplied for the name, so it should be understood as identifying that individual rather than as describing an idea or activity.

Iadou is a proper name, also given as “Iathu.” It identifies a person named in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Nehemiah 12:11. Because the available information provides the name and reference but not the verse text or surrounding passage, its specific role in that verse cannot be described further here. The word itself functions as a personal designation rather than as a general description, action, quality, or theological term.

This noun means “temple robber”: a person who steals from or profanes a temple. It identifies someone by a specific offense involving a sacred place, rather than describing an ordinary thief in general. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 2 Maccabees 4:42. That reference locates its only occurrence, but the precise force of the word in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

Iras is a proper name used to identify a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, so its meaning is the personal designation “Iras.” The name occurs five times in the LXX corpus, appearing in Genesis and 2 Samuel. Its exact identity and role in any particular passage must be understood from that passage’s surrounding text.

Ιωαχας is a personal name, rendered in English as Iōachas or Ioakhas. It identifies a particular person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs 17 times across 16 verses, all in 2 Kings, from 2 Kings 10:35 through 2 Kings 23:34. The name itself does not express a general concept; the surrounding verse is needed to identify which person named Ιωαχας is intended in a particular occurrence.

This noun means “beauty”: an attractive or pleasing quality in a person or thing. It describes outward appearance or the quality that makes someone or something beautiful. The word occurs 50 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, showing regular use for beauty as a recognizable quality rather than a single isolated idea. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek Old Testament noun means “bread-basket,” referring to a container used to hold bread or baked food. It appears twelve times in the Greek Old Testament, especially in passages describing food prepared for presentation, serving, or transport. The word is found from Genesis through Numbers, including instructions connected with offerings and priestly service. Its basic meaning remains practical and concrete: a basket or container associated specifically with bread. The surrounding passage determines whether the basket is being carried, presented, or used in a sacred meal setting.

Kariathiarin is a proper name, preserved as “Kariathiarin.” It functions as a specific name rather than a general description or action word. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, at Joshua 18:14. The available lexical information identifies the name itself, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain whether it names a person, place, or another specific entity. Its exact reference is therefore best understood from Joshua 18:14 in context.

This verb means to trust—to place confidence in someone or something. It describes an act of relying on another rather than merely recognizing or considering that person or thing. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, at Micah 7:5, so its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. Its basic sense remains straightforward: trusting, relying, or putting confidence in the one being considered.

Kaphthoriim, also rendered Kafthorim, is a proper name. It identifies a named group or people in the Greek Old Testament, rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This name appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at Genesis 10:14. Since no verse text or surrounding passage is provided here, the name’s specific role in that verse cannot be described further; its lexical meaning is the name itself: Kaphthoriim or Kafthorim.

This Greek LXX noun means “headband,” a band worn around the head. It names a physical item rather than an action, quality, or person. The word occurs 12 times in the LXX corpus, mostly in Old Testament books, with one occurrence in Sirach. Its precise use in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and description, but its central meaning remains a headband or head covering of that general kind.

This verb means to “bend forward.” It describes the physical action of leaning or inclining the body toward the front. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Job 22:29, so its normal meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not provided here. The word functions as an action word, expressing what someone does rather than naming a person, object, or quality.

This verb means “lap with the tongue,” describing the physical action of using the tongue to take in liquid. It names an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs four times, all within three verses of Judges 7. Its precise force in any one sentence depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning remains this direct bodily action.

This noun means "famine" or "hunger": a serious lack of food that leaves people in need. In the Greek Old Testament, it commonly describes widespread food shortage, though it can also refer to the condition of being hungry. The word occurs 108 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, from Genesis through 1 Maccabees. It is especially frequent in prophetic and historical passages, where famine appears as a recurring human hardship. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

This noun means "Second Quarter," referring to a designated area or district with that name. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in 2 Chronicles 34:22. The word identifies a specific place rather than describing an action, quality, or person. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the place-name usage there; the lexical sense itself remains the name of the Second Quarter.

Matraith, also rendered Matreth, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an idea, action, or quality. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, in Genesis 36:39. The available wording identifies the person by name, but without the verse text it does not establish the name’s personal significance, ancestry, or role. Its meaning is therefore best represented simply as the personal name Matraith or Matreth.

Merathon is a proper name, referring to a person or place identified by that name rather than expressing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 27:30. The available lexical meaning is simply “Merathon”; the name itself does not provide further information about the person or place it identifies. Its precise reference and significance therefore depend on the surrounding verse and passage, not on the name alone.

“Governor” is a noun for a person who governs or administers a territory or people. In the Greek LXX, this word has the clear lexical sense “governor.” It occurs once in the deuterocanonical corpus represented here, in 1 Maccabees 10:65. The word identifies an office or governing role; the surrounding verse would be needed to explain the particular person’s actions or situation.

This noun means “remembrance”: something that causes a person, event, or matter to be remembered. It can describe a memorial or commemorative reminder, and its use may refer to remembering someone before God or preserving a matter for later recall. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, it occurs 71 times, showing that remembrance is a recurring idea across worship, records, offerings, and personal or communal memory. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This word means “branch,” referring to a limb or bough of a tree or shrub. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament, where it appears three times, in Nehemiah and Isaiah. The word’s basic sense is botanical and concrete: a part growing from a woody plant. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and its imagery, but the word itself identifies a branch rather than an abstract quality or action.

Namouēl; Namoil is a proper name for a person. It functions as a personal name rather than describing an object, action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs three times: twice in Numbers and once in 1 Chronicles. The name appears in Numbers 26:9, Numbers 26:12, and 1 Chronicles 4:24. Its exact significance as a name is not defined by the available lexical information, so the surrounding passage is needed to identify the person and understand the reference.

Nataim, also called Natem, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a specific named entity in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 4:23. The available information preserves the name and its alternate form, but does not provide enough verse text to explain more about the person, place, or group it identifies. Its precise significance therefore depends on the surrounding passage.

This LXX word describes someone as an “alien” or “foreigner”—a person regarded as coming from outside a particular people or place. As an adjective, it characterizes a person or thing as foreign rather than belonging to the local community. It occurs 20 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is used across several settings without changing its central idea. The surrounding verse determines the precise force in each occurrence.

This noun means “holocaust” or “whole burnt offering,” referring to a sacrifice offered wholly to God rather than being kept for ordinary use. It belongs to the Greek Old Testament and occurs 83 times, mainly in passages describing Israel’s sacrificial worship. The word appears from Exodus through 1 Maccabees, showing its use across instructions, offerings, and acts of worship. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Opher, also rendered Ofer, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named person or place in the Greek Old Testament translation. The name occurs eight times across eight verses, especially in Numbers, Joshua, and 1 Chronicles. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific referent cannot be identified here, but its lexical function is clear: it serves as a personal or place name preserved as “Opher.”

This Greek LXX noun means a “pattern”—a model, design, or form that can be followed or reproduced. It refers to an arranged example rather than a mere idea, and its use can describe plans for sacred furnishings or other visible forms. The word occurs 12 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun refers to finishing or an end—the point at which something reaches its conclusion. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Ecclesiastes. It can describe the completion or limit of a matter, whether considering what happens during life or the point at which words and efforts come to their close. The basic idea is straightforward: something has reached its finishing point or final boundary. The precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

The verb means “turn dark.” It describes becoming darker rather than naming a person, object, or fixed condition. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs twice: once in Amos and once in Sirach. These occurrences place the word in both Old Testament and deuterocanonical Greek writings, while its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence. Its central idea remains a change toward darkness or a darkened appearance.

This adjective means “very merciful,” describing someone marked by abundant compassion and readiness to show mercy. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used especially in descriptions of God, presenting mercy as a strong and abundant quality rather than a small or occasional response. The word occurs 10 times in the LXX, including passages in Exodus, Numbers, Nehemiah, and Psalms. Its precise force in any individual verse is shaped by the surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains richly and deeply merciful.

This Greek LXX noun means a cup, a vessel used for holding or drinking liquid. It normally refers to an ordinary physical container, whether used in a household setting or as part of furnishings and service. The word appears 32 times across 28 Old Testament verses in the Greek LXX, from Genesis through Habakkuk. Its basic meaning remains straightforward, while the surrounding passage determines whether the cup is being described as an object, measured serving vessel, or symbolic image. It should not be confused with a Greek New Testament word merely because both may be rendered “cup.”

This verb means to forewarn someone of something—to give a warning about what is ahead. It expresses an act of informing another person beforehand, so they are not left unaware of a coming matter. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Ezekiel 33:9. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is clear: warning someone in advance. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that translation corpus.

This noun means “advancement”: movement forward toward a further stage. It describes making headway rather than simply remaining where one is. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, once in Sirach and once in 2 Maccabees. Since the surrounding verse texts are not included, its precise force in either passage depends on the sentence and context. Its central idea remains forward movement or progress.

This adjective describes something that is flaming with fire or blazing. It presents fire as visibly burning intensely, so it can characterize a fiery object or condition rather than naming fire itself. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, in Wisdom and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains something ablaze or burning brightly.

Rhaiphan, also rendered Rhefan, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Amos 5:26. The available wording identifies the name itself but does not provide a further definition or explanation of whom it names. Its specific significance in Amos therefore depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.

Samir is a proper name, referring to a named individual or place in the Greek Old Testament tradition. The word itself supplies a name rather than a descriptive quality, action, or spiritual concept. It appears three times in the Greek LXX corpus, rendered consistently as “Samir.” Its occurrences are found in Joshua 15:48 and Judges 10:1–2, but the surrounding verse text is needed to identify whether each reference concerns a person or a location.

This Greek LXX noun means “decay” or “putrefaction”—the process by which something deteriorates, decomposes, or becomes corrupt. It names a condition of physical breakdown rather than an action someone performs. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach 19:3. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning remains the deterioration or rotting of something.

This verb means “shelter”: to protect or cover someone or something from harm or exposure. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs 38 times, showing repeated use for the act of providing protection. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains giving shelter or covering. The word appears from Exodus through 3 Maccabees, including passages represented in Exodus, Deuteronomy, 1 Samuel, and Nehemiah.

This word means “tent,” referring to a temporary shelter or dwelling made for habitation. As a noun, it names the shelter itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Wisdom 9:15. The surrounding verse text is not available here, so the word’s specific force in that sentence cannot be described further; its ordinary meaning remains a tent or temporary dwelling.

This word means “spark,” referring to a small flash or glowing particle associated with fire. It is a noun, so it names this thing rather than describing an action. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs eight times across Isaiah, Ezekiel, Wisdom, and Sirach. Its uses include both the ordinary image of sparks and figurative comparisons involving something brief, fiery, or easily produced. The precise force in any passage depends on the surrounding verse and its context.

This adjective describes someone or something as pardoned or able to be pardoned. It expresses the idea that a fault, offense, or person may be excused rather than held under lasting condemnation. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, both times in the book of Wisdom, so its recorded use is limited but consistent. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and larger context.

This verb means to sound together—to produce a united or simultaneous sound. It describes sounds joining or being heard in harmony rather than remaining separate. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 6:17. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is the combining of sounds into one coordinated expression.

This adjective describes something vehement or violent—marked by powerful force, intensity, or fierceness. It can characterize an action, movement, or condition that is not mild but forceful and overwhelming. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs six times, with uses ranging from Exodus through 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in any sentence depends on what it describes, but the central idea remains strong, intense force rather than gentleness or restraint.

This Greek verb means to “split” or “cut out.” It describes separating something into parts or removing a portion by cutting. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek books, it is used 11 times, so its basic sense is an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The surrounding wording determines whether the emphasis falls on dividing something apart or cutting a piece away.

This noun means a trophy: an object associated with victory or triumph. It names a visible token of victory rather than an action or feeling. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in 2 Maccabees, at 5:6 and 15:6. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine its particular force in either passage, because context gives the word its specific reference there.

This Greek LXX verb means “sing a hymn”—to express praise or worship through sung words. It describes the act of hymn-singing rather than merely speaking or making music. The word occurs 58 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, showing repeated use for sung praise directed toward God. Its precise emphasis in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central sense remains the same: to sing a hymn of praise. This word is found from Judges through 4 Maccabees.

This verb means to “put under as a support”—to place something beneath another thing so it can hold or support it. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs only twice, once in Job and once in Proverbs. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains placing something underneath as a support.

This Greek LXX verb means to procure something by corruption or to work underhandedly.
